Notes: Year Established -1000 (c.): Jerusalem was the Judahite/Israelite capital from the traditional date of David's conquest (2 Samuel 5:6-9, c. 1000 BCE) through the Iron Age, so Jewish (Judahite) presence long predates 586 BCE. Event 586 BCE: Lipschits (2009) states that 'according to both biblical and archaeological evidence, Jerusalem was destroyed and left deserted by the Babylonians for a period of nearly 50 years', Mizpah serving as capital of Yehud. Population 0 = documented destruction and abandonment per this source (some scholars allow a small residual or cultic presence; not counted here).

Halligan (2002: 146), using Carter's textual formula, estimated 977-1,080 inhabitants in Jerusalem at the beginning of the Persian period (midpoint given); cited by Lipschits 2009 n. 2. Year = start of Persian rule/return under Cyrus, c.

Return from Babylonian exile (Ezra 2:1): exiles 'returned to Jerusalem and Judah, all to their own towns' (c. 538 BCE). Ezra 2:64-65 gives the whole assembly as 42,360 plus 7,337 servants - a figure for all returnees to Judah, not Jerusalem residents; kept out of Population. Ezra 2:70 says priests, Levites and some of the people lived in their towns.

Second Temple completed 'on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius' (Ezra 6:15) = 515 BCE; Jerusalem re-established as the Judean cult centre with a resident priestly community. No numbers.

Carter (1999: 200), from textual evidence in Nehemiah, Haggai and Zechariah 1-8, estimated Jerusalem's population before Nehemiah at 625-750 inhabitants (midpoint given); cited by Lipschits 2009 n. 2. Year = pre-Nehemiah, mid-5th c. BCE, c.
Weinberg (2000: 308-309) hypothesized only 50-150 men (200-600 people) in Jerusalem before Nehemiah's synoikismos (midpoint 400 given); cited by Lipschits 2009 n. 2. Year c. pre-445 BCE.
Zwickel (2008: 216-217), mainly from the lists in Nehemiah, estimated about 200 people in Jerusalem before the days of Nehemiah ('ultra-minimalistic' view); cited by Lipschits 2009. Year c.

Carter (1994; 1999: 148, 288) and Lipschits (2003; 2005; 2006), on archaeological data, estimated ca. 1,500 inhabitants in Jerusalem during the 5th century BCE (c. 60 dunams at 20-25 persons per built-up dunam); cited by Lipschits 2009. Year = 5th c. BCE midpoint.

Nehemiah 7:4 (Nehemiah's governorship, from 445 BCE, after rebuilding the walls): 'The city was wide and large, but the people within it were few, and no houses had been built.' Literary attestation of a small resident Jewish population.

Finkelstein (2008: 501-507): settled area only c. 20-25 dunams of the Southeastern Hill; population during Nehemiah's period about 400 people incl. women and children (c. 100 men); elsewhere 400-500 at 20 persons per built-up dunam (midpoint 450 given). Lipschits notes his own dimensions actually give c. 28.8 dunams = c. 600-720 people. Cited by Lipschits 2009.

Nehemiah 11:1-19: lots cast so that one in ten would live in Jerusalem; residents listed as 468 descendants of Perez, 928 Benjaminites, priests 822 + 242 heads of ancestral houses + 128 warriors, 284 Levites, 172 gatekeepers (sum 3,044, mostly adult men or heads of houses). Ancient list of males; Finkelstein (2010) dates such lists to Hasmonean realities, so not used as Population. Year c. after Nehemiah's synoikismos.

Weinberg (1992: 43; 2000) took the 3,044 men of Nehemiah 11 as Jerusalem's population after Nehemiah's synoikismos = about 12,000 or 15,000 people (midpoint given); textual (maximalist) estimate, rejected by later archaeological estimates. Cited by Lipschits 2009. Year c.
Zwickel (2008): about 400 or 600 people in Jerusalem after Nehemiah's measures (midpoint given); textual estimate cited by Lipschits 2009. Year c.

Lipschits (2009, JHS 9 art. 20): settled area in the Persian and early Hellenistic periods = c. 28-30 dunams on the City of David ridge + c. 20 dunams of the Ophel = c. 50 dunams; at 20-25 persons per built-up dunam = about 1,000-1,250 people (midpoint given). Archaeological area x density estimate. Year = Persian period midpoint (539-332 BCE).

Broshi (1977: 68, table p. 71) estimated Persian-period Jerusalem at approximately 4,800 inhabitants (older estimate, before it was recognised that the city was confined to the Southeastern Hill); cited by Lipschits 2009. Year = Persian period midpoint.
Oeming (1987: 193-194) estimated about 4,800-6,000 people or more in Persian-period Jerusalem (midpoint given); cited by Lipschits 2009. Persian period midpoint.
Levine (2002: 33) estimated about 4,000-5,000 inhabitants in Persian-period Jerusalem (midpoint given); cited by Lipschits 2009. Persian period midpoint.
Blenkinsopp (1988: 320-327) and Grabbe (1998: 59) estimated about 3,000 inhabitants in Persian-period Jerusalem; cited by Lipschits 2009. Persian period midpoint.

Geva (2007b: 56-57, Eretz-Israel 28) estimated about 1,000 people on a settled area of 60 dunams with a low density coefficient; cited by Lipschits 2009. (Shanks, BAR 2016, gives the same Geva figure: about a thousand people on 40 acres.) Persian period midpoint.

Finkelstein (2010, 'Persian Period Jerusalem and Yehud: A Rejoinder', JHS 9 art. 24): Persian-period Jerusalem covered ca. 2-2.5 hectares, i.e. a small settlement of a few hundred people; he sees no reason to change his minimalist view and dates the Nehemiah 3 wall account and the returnee lists to Hasmonean realities. Area only on the fetched page; number covered by the Finkelstein 2008 row.

Elephantine letter (408 BCE per Encyclopaedia Judaica; draft dated 407) to Bagohi governor of Judah mentions an earlier appeal 'to Johanan, the high priest in Jerusalem' and the priests there - contemporary documentary evidence of the Jerusalem high priesthood and priestly community.
Broshi estimated c. 4,500 people in Jerusalem around 333 BCE (vs. 25,000 under Hezekiah); per Wikipedia (note 20), original not checked. Year c. 333 BCE.

Ptolemy I son of Lagus seized Jerusalem by treachery on a Sabbath, ruled it cruelly, and took many captives from the mountainous parts of Judea, the places about Jerusalem, Samaria and Gerizim to Egypt (Josephus, Antiquities 12.1.1; also Agatharchides in Against Apion 1.22). Date c. 312 BCE (variously 320-302). No numbers.

Hecataeus of Abdera (c. 300 BCE, quoted by Josephus, Against Apion 1.22 sect. 197): Jerusalem, 'about fifty furlongs in circumference, which is inhabited by a hundred and twenty thousand men, or thereabouts'. Ancient figure, far above all archaeological estimates (c. 1,000-5,000 for this period) and of disputed authenticity (Pseudo-Hecataeus); Population left blank.

Ben Sira 50:1-4: Simon son of Onias, high priest (c. 200 BCE), repaired the temple and 'fortified the city against siege' - literary attestation of the Jewish temple city in the early Hellenistic period. Year c.

Antiochus III, after taking Jerusalem (c. 200-198 BCE), wrote of his intention 'to retrieve the condition of their city, which hath been greatly depopulated' and 'to bring those that have been scattered abroad back to the city' (Josephus, Antiquities 12.3.3). Event: depopulation and resettlement; no numbers.

2 Maccabees 5:11-14: Antiochus IV took Jerusalem by storm (169/168 BCE); 'eighty thousand were destroyed, forty thousand in hand-to-hand fighting', and as many sold into slavery. Ancient casualty/captive figure, generally regarded as exaggerated; kept out of Population.

1 Maccabees 1:29-38: the king's chief collector of tribute attacked Jerusalem, plundered and burned it, tore down houses and walls, fortified the City of David as a citadel (the Akra), and 'the residents of Jerusalem fled'. Event c. 167 BCE.

1 Maccabees 3:45: 'Jerusalem was uninhabited like a wilderness; not one of her children went in or out' (c. 166/165 BCE). Poetic lament; Hellenizing Jews and the Seleucid garrison remained in the Akra (1 Macc 6:21), so not treated as documented total absence; Population blank.
1 Maccabees 4:52-53: rededication of the altar on 25 Chislev, year 148 SE (December 164 BCE) - Judean (Maccabean) control of the Temple restored.

1 Maccabees 13:49-52: Simon took the citadel (Akra) of Jerusalem on 23 Iyyar, year 171 SE (141 BCE); he and his men lived there - end of the Seleucid/Hellenizers' enclave, city wholly under Hasmonean Jewish rule.

Geva's population estimate for Hasmonean (late Hellenistic) Jerusalem, 150-50 BCE: 8,000 (from Geva, Tel Aviv 41, 2014, minimalist archaeological view), reported by H. Shanks, BAR May/June 2016. Year = midpoint of 150-50 BCE.
Broshi estimated the population of Hasmonean Jerusalem at 30,000-35,000 (midpoint given); per Wikipedia (note 40), original not checked. Year = Hasmonean period midpoint (140-37 BCE).

Alexander Jannaeus crucified about 800 of his Jewish opponents 'in the sight of all the city' of Jerusalem and had their wives and children killed; about 8,000 opponents fled (Josephus, Antiquities 13.14.2). Date c. 88 BCE. Victims and fugitives, not residents counted.

Ritual baths: about 150 miqvaot found in Jerusalem, about 60 in the Upper City (Avigad's Jewish Quarter excavations) and about 40 near the southern gates of the Temple Mount, dated to the later Second Temple period (2nd c. BCE-1st c. CE) - R. Reich, 'The Great Mikveh Debate', BAR 19:2 (1993). Archaeological evidence of a large, purity-observant Jewish population. Year = midpoint of 2nd c. BCE-1st c. CE range, c.
Pompey's capture of the Temple (63 BCE): 'of the Jews were slain twelve thousand' (Josephus, War 1.7.5). Death toll; not a population figure.

Herod, in the eighteenth year of his reign (c. 20/19 BCE), began rebuilding the Temple, employing 10,000 skilled workmen and training about 1,000 priests as builders (Josephus, Antiquities 15.11.1-2). Workforce figures, not population.

Joachim Jeremias, Jerusalem in the Time of Jesus (1962, pp. 79-83): normal population about 55,000, plus some 125,000 Passover visitors (visitors excluded); as reported by Christian Courier (secondary, non-academic page). Year = time of Jesus, c. 30 CE.
Jeremias's revised estimate (1966/1969, p. 84): normal population of Jerusalem only 25,000-30,000 at the upper limit (midpoint given); as reported by Christian Courier. c. 30 CE.

A. Edersheim, Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah (orig. 1883; ed. 1947 p. 116): population of New Testament-era Jerusalem approximately 250,000 (old, maximalist estimate, superseded); as reported by Christian Courier. c. 30 CE.

Acts 2:5 'devout Jews from every people under heaven living in Jerusalem' and Acts 6:9 'the synagogue of the Freedmen... Cyrenians, Alexandrians' and Jews of Cilicia and Asia: New Testament attestation of resident Diaspora-born Jewish communities with their own synagogue(s), c. 30-35 CE.

Theodotos inscription (Frey, CIJ II 1404; translation by S. Berrin on the page): Greek dedication by Theodotos son of Vettenus, priest and archisynagogue, grandson of an archisynagogue, who built a synagogue for reading the Law and teaching the commandments with a guest-house and water installations for strangers; dated mid-1st c. CE, before 70 - evidence of a Greek-speaking (Diaspora-origin) Jewish congregation resident in Jerusalem over three generations. Year c.

Josephus, War 6.9.3: under Cestius Gallus (c. 65/66 CE) the high priests counted 256,500 Passover sacrifices, which at ten persons per lamb Josephus turns into 2,700,200 pure persons. Pilgrim crowd from all Judea and the Diaspora, not residents; universally regarded as exaggerated.

Outbreak of the Great Revolt in Jerusalem (66 CE): Eleazar son of Ananias, governor of the Temple, persuaded the priests to accept no sacrifice for any foreigner, 'the true beginning of our war with the Romans' (Josephus, War 2.17.2).

Geva (Tel Aviv 41, 2014, archaeological minimalist view) estimates Herodian/early Roman Jerusalem at 20,000, i.e. at most 20,000 before the 70 CE destruction; reported by H. Shanks, BAR 2016, who notes other scholars' estimates of 25,000-75,000, around 75,000, over 100,000 and nearly a quarter million. Year = eve of the revolt, c.

R. Reich, 'A note on the population size of Jerusalem in the Second Temple period', Revue Biblique 121 (2014) 298-305: around 30,000 people, at 500 persons per hectare of residential area, linked to the growth enclosed by the Second Wall (Wikipedia gives his figure as 28,600). Late Second Temple period; year c. eve of revolt.

Broshi (1978, BAR 4:2 'Estimating the Population of Ancient Jerusalem'): 80,000 for Jerusalem at its greatest extent before the destruction (area x density); listed by Wikipedia under the 70 CE siege. Resident estimate, year c. 66 (pre-siege).

J. Wilkinson (1974, 'Ancient Jerusalem: Its Water Supply and Population', PEQ 106: 33-51): 70,398, derived from water-supply capacity (criticised by Broshi for an arbitrary 20 litres/person/day). Listed by Wikipedia for 70 CE; year c. 66 (pre-siege).

L. I. Levine (2002, Jerusalem: Portrait of the City, quoted in Rocca 2008: 333): 60,000-70,000 (midpoint given), assuming the Third Wall area held half the population of the rest of the city. Listed by Wikipedia for 70 CE; year c. 66.

W. Reinhardt (1995, p. 263) suggested 100,000-120,000 for pre-revolt Jerusalem (midpoint given); per Wikipedia, which notes modern estimates range from 20,000 to around 100,000 (Price 2011). Original not checked.
E. Lipiński (2007, p. 9): 35,000-40,000 for pre-revolt Jerusalem (midpoint given); per Wikipedia, original not checked.
J. Strange (2003, p. 110): 75,000 for pre-revolt Jerusalem; per Wikipedia, original not checked.

Tacitus, Histories 5.13: 'the total number of the besieged, of every age and both sexes, amounted to six hundred thousand'. Ancient figure for those trapped in the siege (incl. pilgrims and refugees), treated as exaggerated by modern scholars (resident estimates 20,000-80,000).

Josephus, War 6.9.3: 97,000 captives taken in the whole war and 1,100,000 perished during the siege, 'the greater part of whom were indeed of the same nation, but not belonging to the city itself', having come for Passover. Casualty and captive figures, regarded as greatly exaggerated (Broshi); not residents.

Burnt House (Upper City): residence with a small miqveh, stone vessels and a stone weight inscribed '(of) Bar Kathros' (priestly family); numerous coins of the revolt (66-70 CE) date its destruction - 'evidence was found of the total destruction of the city by the Romans in the year 70 CE'. Herodian Quarter houses had one or two or more miqvaot each. Archaeological evidence of the Jewish residential quarter up to its destruction.

Destruction (August-September 70 CE): when the army 'had no more people to slay or to plunder, because there remained none', Titus ordered the entire city and temple demolished except three towers and the western wall, so that 'there was left nothing to make those that came thither believe it had ever been inhabited'; the Tenth Legion was left as garrison (Josephus, War 7.1.1-2). Population 0 = ancient statement that no inhabitants remained; some scholars allow a small residual Jewish presence after 70.
